title: Chapter XIV
paragraphs: As soon as I had read the letter, I went to the master. I told him that his sister had arrived at the Heights and had written to express her sorrow at Mrs. Linton's illness and her intense wish to see him. She hoped he would send her some sign of forgiveness through me as soon as possible.

“Forgiveness!” Linton said. “I have nothing to forgive her for, Ellen. You may go to Wuthering Heights this afternoon if you like. Tell her I'm not _angry_, but _sad_ to have lost her, especially as I cannot believe she will ever be happy. But visiting her is out of the question. We are separated for ever. If she truly wants to please me, let her persuade the villain she has married to leave the country.”
“Won't you write her just a little note, sir?” I asked pleadingly.
“No,” he answered. “There's no need. I shall have as little contact with Heathcliff's family as he has with mine. None at all!”

Mr. Edgar's coldness made me deeply unhappy. All the way from the Grange, I tried to think how I could put more warmth into his words when I repeated them, and soften his refusal to write even a few comforting lines to Isabella. I imagine she had been watching for me since morning. As I came up the paved garden path I saw her at the window and nodded, but she drew back as though afraid of being seen. I went in without knocking. Never had I seen such a dreary, miserable sight as that once cheerful house! I confess that, in the young lady's place, I would at least have swept the hearth and wiped the tables. But she had already caught the general spirit of neglect around her. Her pretty face was pale and lifeless, and her hair had not been curled: some strands hung straight down, while others were carelessly twisted round her head. She probably hadn't touched her clothes since the previous evening. Hindley was absent. Mr. Heathcliff sat at a table looking through papers in his pocketbook. When I appeared he got up, greeted me quite pleasantly, and offered me a chair. He was the only decent-looking thing in the room, and I thought I had never seen him look better. Circumstances had so reversed their positions that a stranger would certainly have taken him for a gentleman born and bred, and his wife for a thoroughly slovenly little creature! She hurried to greet me, holding out one hand for the letter she expected. I shook my head. She refused to understand, followed me to the sideboard where I put my bonnet, and whispered urgently that I must give her what I had brought. Heathcliff guessed what she was doing. “If you've brought anything for Isabella—and no doubt you have, Nelly—give it to her,” he said. “There's no need for secrecy. We have no secrets from each other.”

“Oh, I haven't brought anything,” I answered, deciding it was best to tell the truth at once. “My master asked me to tell his sister that she must expect neither a letter nor a visit from him for the present. He sends his love, ma'am, and his hopes for your happiness, and forgives you for the pain you've caused him. But he thinks that from now on the two households should have no contact, since nothing can come of keeping it up.”

Mrs. Heathcliff's lip trembled a little, and she went back to her seat by the window. Her husband stood near me on the hearth and began asking about Catherine. I told him as much about her illness as I thought proper, and his insistent questioning dragged out most of the facts about how it began. I blamed her, as she deserved, for bringing it on herself. I ended by saying I hoped he would follow Mr. Linton's example and stop interfering with the family, whether for good or ill.

“Mrs. Linton is only just recovering,” I said. “She'll never be what she was, but her life has been spared. If you really care for her, you'll keep out of her way—more than that, you'll leave this part of the country altogether. And so that you won't regret going, I'll tell you that Catherine Linton is now as different from your old friend Catherine Earnshaw as that young lady is from me. Her looks have changed greatly, and her character still more. Whoever is obliged to share her life will only be able to keep loving her through memories of what she once was, through ordinary human kindness, and through a sense of duty!”

“Quite possible,” Heathcliff said, forcing himself to appear calm. “Quite possible that your master has nothing left but ordinary human kindness and a sense of duty. But do you think I'll leave Catherine to his _duty_ and _kindness_? Can you compare what I feel for her with what he feels? Before you leave this house, you must promise to arrange a meeting for me with her. Whether you agree or refuse, I _will_ see her! What do you say?”
“I say, Mr. Heathcliff, that you mustn't,” I answered. “And you'll never do it through me. Another clash between you and the master would kill her outright.”

“With your help we can avoid that,” he continued. “And if there were any danger of such a clash—if he caused her one more moment of trouble—well, I think I would be justified in going to extremes! I wish you were honest enough to tell me whether Catherine would suffer greatly if she lost him. The fear that she would is what holds me back. There's the difference between our feelings. If he had been in my place and I in his, even if my hatred of him had poisoned my whole life, I would never have lifted a hand against him. Look as unbelieving as you please! I would never have driven him out of her company while she wanted him there. The moment she stopped caring for him, I would have torn out his heart and drunk his blood! But until then—if you don't believe me, you don't know me—until then, I would have died inch by inch before touching a hair on his head!”

“And yet,” I interrupted, “you feel no hesitation about destroying every hope of her full recovery. Just when she has almost forgotten you, you mean to force yourself back into her thoughts and plunge her into another storm of quarrelling and misery.”

“You think she's almost forgotten me?” he said. “Oh, Nelly! You know she hasn't! You know as well as I do that for every thought she gives Linton she gives a thousand to me! At the most miserable time of my life I did think something like that. It haunted me when I came back here last summer. But nothing except hearing it from her own lips could make me believe that dreadful idea again. And then Linton would mean nothing, nor Hindley, nor any dream I've ever had. My future would come down to two words: _death_ and _hell_. Living after losing her would be hell. Yet I was a fool to imagine for a moment that Edgar Linton's love meant more to her than mine. If he loved her with every power of his feeble little being, he couldn't love as much in eighty years as I could in one day. And Catherine's heart is as deep as mine. You could fit the sea into that horse trough as easily as he could claim all her love. Nonsense! He's hardly more precious to her than her dog or her horse. He hasn't it in him to be loved as I am. How can she love something in him that he doesn't possess?”
“Catherine and Edgar love each other as much as any two people can,” Isabella cried, suddenly roused. “Nobody has the right to speak like that, and I won't sit quietly while you belittle my brother!”
“Your brother is wonderfully fond of you too, isn't he?” Heathcliff remarked scornfully. “He's been surprisingly quick to turn you loose in the world.”
“He doesn't know what I'm suffering,” she answered. “I didn't tell him.”
“So you have told him something? You've written to him, have you?”
“I wrote to say I was married. You saw the note.”
“And you've written nothing since?”
“No, nothing.”
“My young lady looks sadly the worse for being married,” I observed. “Clearly someone's love has failed her. I can guess whose, though perhaps I'd better not say.”

“I'd guess it's her own,” said Heathcliff. “She's turning into a complete sloven! She's given up trying to please me remarkably soon. You'd hardly believe it, but the very day after our wedding she was crying to go home. Still, being less particular will make her fit into this house all the better. And I'll see that she doesn't disgrace me by wandering outside.”

“Well, sir,” I replied, “I hope you'll remember that Mrs. Heathcliff is used to being cared for and waited on. She was brought up as an only daughter, with everyone ready to serve her. You must give her a maid to keep things tidy for her, and you must treat her kindly. Whatever you think of Mr. Edgar, you cannot doubt that she is capable of deep affection. Otherwise she would never have given up the elegance, comforts, and friends of her old home to settle happily with you in a wilderness like this.”

“She gave them up under a delusion,” he answered. “She pictured me as the hero of a romance, whose chivalrous devotion would grant her every whim. I can hardly think of her as a rational creature: she was so stubborn about inventing a fanciful version of my character and acting on the false notions she treasured. But at last I think she's beginning to know me. I no longer see the foolish smiles and grimaces that first irritated me, or that senseless inability to understand that I meant what I said about her infatuation and about her. It was a marvellous feat of insight when she discovered that I didn't love her. At one point I thought no lesson would ever teach her that! Even now she hasn't learnt it properly. This morning she informed me, as though announcing something appalling, that I'd actually succeeded in making her hate me! A labour worthy of Hercules, I assure you! If I've managed it, I have reason to give thanks. Can I believe you, Isabella? Are you certain you hate me? If I leave you alone for half a day, won't you come sighing and coaxing me again? I expect she'd rather I had shown nothing but tenderness in front of you. Having the truth exposed hurts her vanity. But I don't care who knows that the passion was entirely on one side, and I never lied to her about it. She can't accuse me of showing the least false tenderness. The first thing she saw me do when we left the Grange was hang her little dog. When she begged for its life, my first words were that I wished I could hang every creature belonging to her, except one. Perhaps she imagined she was the exception. Yet no cruelty disgusted her. I suppose she naturally admires it, provided her own precious person is safe from harm! Wasn't it utterly absurd—sheer idiocy—for that pitiful, grovelling, mean-spirited bitch to dream that I could love her? Tell your master, Nelly, that I've never met anything so abject in my life. She even disgraces the name of Linton. Sometimes I've stopped experimenting on how much she can bear before she comes crawling shamefully back, simply because I've run out of ideas! But tell him this too, to reassure both the brother and the magistrate in him: I keep strictly within the law. So far I've carefully avoided giving her the slightest legal grounds for a separation. What's more, she wouldn't thank anyone for parting us. She could go if she wanted. The nuisance of having her here is greater than the pleasure of tormenting her!”

“Mr. Heathcliff,” I said, “you talk like a madman. Your wife probably believes you are mad, and that's why she has endured you until now. But since you say she may leave, I'm sure she'll take the opportunity. You're not so bewitched, ma'am, that you'd stay with him of your own free will?”

“Be careful, Ellen!” Isabella answered, her eyes blazing with anger. Their expression left no doubt that her husband had fully succeeded in making her detest him. “Don't believe a single word he says. He's a lying devil! A monster, not a human being! He's told me before that I could leave, and I tried, but I daren't try again! Only promise, Ellen, that you won't repeat a syllable of his vile talk to my brother or Catherine. Whatever he pretends, he wants to drive Edgar to desperation. He says he married me to gain power over him, and he shan't have it. I'll die first! I only hope, I pray, that he'll forget his devilish caution and kill me! The only happiness I can imagine is dying myself or seeing him dead!”

“There, that's enough for now!” Heathcliff said. “If you're called to give evidence in court, Nelly, remember her words! And look carefully at her face: she's almost reached the state that would suit me. No, Isabella, you're no longer fit to look after yourself. As your legal protector, I must keep you in my custody, however unpleasant that duty may be. Go upstairs. I want a private word with Ellen Dean. That's not the way. Upstairs, I said! Why, child, this is the way upstairs!”

He grabbed her and pushed her out of the room. When he came back he was muttering, “I have no pity! None! The more the worms wriggle, the more I want to crush their guts out! It's like teething in the soul: the worse the pain gets, the harder I grind.”
“Do you even understand the word pity?” I asked, hurrying to put on my bonnet. “Have you ever felt a trace of it in your life?”

“Put that down!” he interrupted, seeing that I meant to leave. “You're not going yet. Come here, Nelly. I must either persuade you or force you to help me see Catherine, and without delay. I swear I mean no harm. I don't want to cause a disturbance, or anger or insult Mr. Linton. I only want to hear from her own lips how she is and why she's been ill, and ask whether there's anything I can do for her. I spent six hours in the Grange garden last night, and I'll be back tonight. I'll haunt the place every night and every day until I find a way inside. If Edgar Linton comes across me, I won't hesitate to knock him down and give him enough to keep him quiet while I'm there. If his servants try to stop me, I'll frighten them off with these pistols. But wouldn't it be better to prevent me from meeting either them or their master? You could manage it so easily. I'd let you know when I arrived; then, as soon as she was alone, you could admit me without anyone seeing and keep watch until I left. Your conscience could be perfectly clear: you'd be preventing trouble.”

I protested that I would not betray my employer in his own house. I also insisted on the cruelty and selfishness of disturbing Mrs. Linton's peace merely to satisfy himself. “The most ordinary things give her a painful shock,” I said. “Her nerves are shattered, and I'm certain she couldn't bear the surprise. Don't insist, sir! If you do, I'll have to tell my master what you're planning, and he'll take steps to protect his house and everyone in it from such an outrageous intrusion!”

“In that case I'll take steps to keep you here, woman!” Heathcliff exclaimed. “You won't leave Wuthering Heights until tomorrow morning. It's ridiculous to claim that Catherine couldn't bear to see me. And I don't want to surprise her. You must prepare her—ask her whether I may come. You say she never mentions my name and nobody mentions me to her. Who could she speak to about me if I'm a forbidden subject in the house? She thinks you're all spying for her husband. Oh, I've no doubt she's in hell among you! Her silence tells me as much as anything else how she feels. You say she often looks restless and anxious. Is that proof she's at peace? You talk about her disturbed mind. How the devil could it be anything else, shut away in that dreadful loneliness? With that insipid, worthless creature nursing her out of _duty_ and _human kindness_! Out of _pity_ and _charity_! He might as well plant an oak in a flowerpot and expect it to flourish as think she can grow strong again in the shallow soil of his concerns! We'll settle this now. Will you stay here while I fight my way past Linton and his servant to Catherine? Or will you be my friend, as you always have been, and do what I ask? Decide! If you insist on being stubborn and spiteful, there's no reason for me to wait another minute!”

Well, Mr. Lockwood, I argued, complained, and refused him outright fifty times, but in the end he forced me to agree. I undertook to carry a letter to my mistress. If she consented, I promised to tell him when Linton would next be away, so he could come and get inside as best he could. I wouldn't be there, and the other servants would also be out of the way. Was that right or wrong? I'm afraid it was wrong, though it seemed practical. I thought that giving in would prevent another explosion. I also thought it might bring a helpful turning point in Catherine's mental illness. Then I remembered Mr. Edgar's stern rebuke for carrying tales. I tried to soothe my misgivings by assuring myself again and again that this betrayal of trust—if it deserved such a harsh name—would be my last. Even so, my walk home was sadder than my journey there, and I had many doubts before I could bring myself to place the letter in Mrs. Linton's hand.
But Kenneth is here. I'll go down and tell him how much better you are. My story is _dree_, as we say—long and drawn out—and will help pass another morning.

Dree, and dreary! I thought, as the good woman went downstairs to meet the doctor. Hardly the sort of entertainment I would have chosen, either. But never mind! I'll make wholesome medicine from Mrs. Dean's bitter herbs. First of all, I must guard against the fascination in Catherine Heathcliff's shining eyes. I would be in a pretty predicament if I gave my heart to that young woman and the daughter proved to be another version of her mother.
